Monotone Number Sequences

SequencesCountingLogic
Game: Fill every box with a number so that no four numbers, read from left to right, keep going up or keep going down.
How to play: Click a number and then a box to put it there, or drag the number into a box. Click a number in a box to pick it up again.
Length of sequence
Look for the math

You have as many boxes as numbers. It sounds easy to spread them out so that no four form a steady run — but with ten numbers it cannot be done at all. With nine it can.

What counts as a run

A run is a subsequence: pick any four boxes in order, not necessarily touching, and read their numbers. If those four keep getting bigger (2, 4, 7, 9) or keep getting smaller (9, 7, 4, 2), the board has a fault and those boxes light up. For example, 3, 2, 1, 6, 5, 4, 9, 8, 7 has no such run: each group of three falls, and the groups rise from one to the next.

Why ten always fails

Give every number two labels: how long its longest rising run ending there is, and how long its longest falling run ending there is. If no four ever make a run, each label can only be 1, 2 or 3, so there are just 3 × 3 = 9 different label pairs. With ten numbers, two must share the same pair by the pigeonhole principle — and the later one then gets a longer run than the earlier one, a contradiction. This is the Erdős–Szekeres theorem: any (r−1)(s−1)+1 distinct numbers contain a rising run of length r or a falling one of length s; with r = s = 4 that is ten.

What the check found

The logic test looks at every way to fill the boxes. All 9! = 362,880 arrangements of nine numbers are checked and exactly 1,764 of them work. All 10! = 3,628,800 arrangements of ten are checked and not one works — so the applet's claim is confirmed, not just assumed.

Try the nine-number board above, then swap two neighbours. Can you find a second arrangement that works?
